lead: The World Wide Web uses the HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to let a browser ask a server for a resource and to receive the resource back. HTTP is a request‑response protocol that works over TCP. It is the backbone of web browsing, mobile apps, and many cloud services. Understanding URLs, methods, status codes, headers and the stateless nature of HTTP lets you build clients, debug traffic, and design efficient web services.
prereq: You need: transport services from socket programming and name resolution from DNS.

sections.h3: Uniform Resource Locator and request line

blocks.text: A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) tells the browser where a resource lives. The general form is scheme://host[:port]/path?query#fragment.

scheme is usually http or https. host is a domain name such as example.com. host may be a domain name or an IP address (e.g., 93.184.216.34). port is optional; the default for http is 80 and for https is 443.
path identifies the file on the server, for example /index.html. query is a string after ?, used to pass parameters. fragment after # is processed only by the browser.
When the browser wants a resource it creates a request line. The line has three parts: METHOD SP REQUEST-URI SP HTTP-VERSION CRLF.

blocks.where: GET is the method; /index.html is the request‑URI; HTTP/1.1 is the protocol version.

items: METHOD is a verb such as GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.
SP is a single space character.
CRLF is carriage‑return followed by line‑feed.

blocks.text: GET asks the server to return a representation of the target resource without changing server state.
POST sends data to the server, often causing a change such as creating a new record.
PUT replaces the entire target resource with the supplied representation.

items: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent – repeating the same request has the same effect as a single request.
POST is not idempotent – each repeat may create a new record.

blocks.text: HEAD and OPTIONS are also idempotent because they do not modify server state.
After the request line the server sends a status line: HTTP-VERSION SP STATUS-CODE SP REASON-PHRASE CRLF.

items: 200 OK – request succeeded and response contains the requested data.
404 Not Found – the target resource does not exist.
500 Internal Server Error – server failed to fulfil a valid request.

blocks.text: Headers are key‑value pairs that appear after the request or status line and before an empty line.
Common request headers: Host, User-Agent, Accept, Content-Type. Common response headers: Content-Type, Content-Length, Set-Cookie.
HTTP is stateless. The server does not remember previous requests from the same client unless the client sends a cookie or uses authentication tokens.
HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection for each request. HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections by default.
In HTTP/1.1 the connection is persistent by default; the Connection: keep-alive header is only needed for HTTP/1.0 or to override a default close behavior.

items: Connection: keep-alive tells the server to keep the socket open after the response.
Connection: close forces the server to close the socket after the response.

blocks.text: A persistent connection reduces latency because the TCP three‑way handshake is performed only once.

blocks.where: RTT is round‑trip time in seconds; Size is object size in bytes; Bandwidth is link capacity in bits per second.

blocks.text: HTTPS adds TLS encryption on top of HTTP. Only a few syllabi cover it, so it is mentioned here as a future topic.

examples.question: A laptop requests http://example.com/index.html. The network RTT is 120 ms. The server sends a 1.2 KB HTML page. The link bandwidth is 2 Mbps. Compute the total time from sending the request to receiving the complete page using a persistent connection.
steps: Convert the object size to bits: 1.2 KB × 1024 B/KB × 8 bits/B = 9 830 bits.
Transmission time = size ÷ bandwidth = 9 830 bits ÷ 2 000 000 bits/s = 0.004915 s = 4.915 ms.
Two RTTs are needed (request and first byte of response): 2 × 120 ms = 240 ms.
examples.answer: The page is received in about 245 ms.
examples.check:
rtt = 120.0
size_kb = 1.2
bandwidth_mbps = 2.0
size_bits = size_kb * 1024 * 8
trans_time_ms = (size_bits / (bandwidth_mbps * 1e6)) * 1000
total_ms = 2 * rtt + trans_time_ms
print(round(total_ms,1))

traps: Confusing GET with POST as a safe method; GET must not change server state.
Assuming all HTTP methods are idempotent; only GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS are.
Ignoring the effect of persistent connections and counting only one RTT; the formula needs two RTTs for request and first byte.
Treating the URL fragment (#section) as part of the request sent to the server; it is processed only by the browser.

quiz.q: What does the acronym HTTP stand for?
Explain why HTTP is called a stateless protocol.
quiz.a: Each request contains all information needed to understand it; the server does not retain any client-specific context between requests unless the client sends a cookie or token.

quiz.q: A client sends a POST request with a payload of 500 bytes. The RTT is 80 ms and the link bandwidth is 1 Mbps. Compute the time to receive the complete response if the server replies with a 2 KB page.
quiz.a: Payload bits = 500×8 = 4000 bits. Transmission of request = 4000 ÷ 1 000 000 = 0.004 s = 4 ms. Response bits = 2048×8 = 16384 bits. Transmission of response = 16384 ÷ 1 000 000 = 0.016384 s = 16.4 ms. Total time = 2×80 ms + 4 ms + 16.4 ms ≈ 180.4 ms.

quiz.q:
Given the following HTTP response header, identify which header tells the client how many bytes to read and which header can be used to keep the connection open for further requests:
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1024
Connection: keep-alive
quiz.a: Content-Length tells the client that 1024 bytes follow. Connection: keep-alive indicates that the TCP connection should remain open for additional requests.

quiz.q: Which HTTP status code indicates that the requested resource was not found?
List two differences between HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 regarding connections.
quiz.a: HTTP/1.0 closes the TCP connection after each request unless Connection: keep-alive is used. HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default, so the connection stays open unless Connection: close is sent.

quiz.q: A browser wants to retrieve a resource that requires authentication. Which header is used to send credentials after the first 401 challenge?
If a client repeatedly sends identical GET requests to the same URL, why might the server still return different responses?
quiz.a: Because the server may embed dynamic data such as timestamps, session‑specific content, or vary the response based on cookies or load‑balancing decisions, even though GET is idempotent.

beyond: Not for the exam. HTTP/2 introduces binary framing, header compression and multiplexed streams over a single connection, improving latency for modern browsers. HTTP/3 moves the transport layer to QUIC, a UDP‑based protocol that reduces connection setup time. Research on server push, edge caching, and zero‑RTT TLS aims to make web pages load faster on mobile networks. To explore further, search for "HTTP/2 multiplexing" and "QUIC protocol".
